title: Interpretable Memory Models for Spaced Repetition
summary: Spaced repetition software schedules reviews with a memory model fit to review logs. Accuracy on a test set is not sufficient evidence of quality since available data are produced by existing schedulers, and new solutions must extrapolate beyond them. A model also needs a simple mechanistic interpretation. We present SBD, a model that is more interpretable and 80% smaller than the current state of the art at nearly the same accuracy.

AI.tldr: The authors present SBD, a spaced-repetition memory model that is 80% smaller and more interpretable than the state of the art while achieving nearly the same accuracy.
AI.motivation: Spaced repetition software fits memory models to review logs, but test-set accuracy is insufficient evidence of quality: the data come from existing schedulers, so new methods must extrapolate beyond them. Models also need a simple mechanistic interpretation, which current state-of-the-art approaches often lack.
AI.method: The authors propose SBD, a compact and interpretable memory model for spaced-repetition scheduling, designed to extrapolate beyond data produced by existing schedulers rather than merely fit them.
AI.result: SBD achieves nearly the same accuracy as the current state of the art while being 80% smaller and more interpretable.
AI.conclusion: A smaller, mechanistically interpretable model can match state-of-the-art accuracy, offering a better foundation for spaced-repetition scheduling.

title: The Hill numbers synthesize and generalize measures of trait polygenicity
summary: Characterizing the genetic architecture of phenotypic variation is central to human genetics, yet trait polygenicity---the diversity of genetic variants responsible for a heritable trait's variation in a sample---is rarely quantified formally. O'Connor and Sella (2026) addressed this need by proposing four polygenicity measures that are quasi-arithmetic means and therefore satisfy a set of principles they argue are desirable for polygenicity measures. Here, I show that these four measures are points on a continuum corresponding to the Hill numbers, a family of ecological diversity statistics offering a tunable emphasis on variants with small versus large contributions. I further show that the Hill numbers are the only quasi-arithmetic means suitable for measuring polygenicity because they are the only ones that are "effective numbers" of variants. The connection to the Hill numbers clarifies the relationships among O'Connor and Sella's four polygenicity measures: all four are effective numbers of variants, and those that give greater weight to variants with small contributions yield higher estimates of polygenicity. It also connects polygenicity to results in the ecological diversity literature, including the replication principle, a criterion for how such measures should behave when independent sets of variants are combined. Together, these results offer a unified framework for interpreting, comparing, and selecting measures of trait polygenicity.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that O'Connor and Sella's (2026) four polygenicity measures are Hill numbers, a family of ecological diversity statistics, and that Hill numbers are the only quasi-arithmetic means suitable as "effective numbers" of variants, providing a unified framework for measuring trait polygenicity.
AI.motivation: Trait polygenicity—the diversity of genetic variants underlying a heritable trait—is rarely quantified formally. O'Connor and Sella (2026) proposed four measures based on quasi-arithmetic means satisfying desirable principles, but the relationships among these measures and their deeper justification remained unclear.
AI.method: The author demonstrates mathematically that the four polygenicity measures correspond to points on a continuum defined by the Hill numbers, and proves that Hill numbers are the only quasi-arithmetic means that qualify as "effective numbers" of variants.
AI.result: All four of O'Connor and Sella's measures are effective numbers of variants, with measures weighting small-contribution variants more heavily yielding higher polygenicity estimates. The Hill number framework also links polygenicity to ecological diversity results, including the replication principle for combining independent variant sets.
AI.conclusion: The Hill numbers offer a unified framework for interpreting, comparing, and selecting measures of trait polygenicity, connecting human genetics to ecological diversity theory.

title: MD-LLM-2: A Transferable Language Model of Molecular Dynamics with Physical Conditioning and Explicit Path Probabilities
summary: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations model the motion of proteins between conformational states, but crossing free energy barriers and sampling multiple thermodynamic conditions remain computationally costly. We recently introduced MD-LLM-1, which showed that language models can generate conformational trajectories at lower cost, but required a separate model for each protein and did not explicitly model thermodynamics or kinetics. Here we introduce MD-LLM-2, a transferable language model that generates trajectories conditioned on sequence, temperature and molecular history. Because each step defines a normalized distribution over structural tokens, the model assigns an explicit likelihood to every generated or simulated trajectory. Trained across mdCATH domains, MD-LLM-2 reproduces the median radius of gyration of MD within 1 Angstrom in 10 of 12 unseen domains, predicts reduced Trp-cage compaction at higher temperature, and generates L99A T4 lysozyme trajectories that reach published transition-region backbone structures. In alanine dipeptide simulations, conditioning on a torsional scaling parameter $λ$ predicts basin populations at unseen couplings with a mean absolute error of 0.09 versus 0.35 for MBAR, and first-passage probabilities with an error of 0.08 versus 0.16 for a reversible Markov state model. Frame-isoentropic sampling further limits the accumulation of errors during autoregressive trajectory generation. Together, these results extend MD-LLM from protein-specific trajectory generation to transferable, physically conditioned modelling with explicit path likelihoods, and show that the framework can predict equilibrium populations for force-field parameters not seen during training, with an initial indication that first-passage kinetics can also be captured.

AI.tldr: MD-LLM-2 is a transferable language model that generates protein conformational trajectories conditioned on sequence, temperature, and molecular history, providing explicit path likelihoods and predicting equilibrium and kinetic properties across unseen conditions.
AI.motivation: Molecular dynamics simulations of protein motion are computationally costly, especially for crossing free energy barriers and sampling multiple thermodynamic conditions. Prior work (MD-LLM-1) could generate trajectories cheaply but needed a separate model per protein and did not explicitly model thermodynamics or kinetics.
AI.method: MD-LLM-2 is a transferable language model trained across mdCATH domains that generates trajectories conditioned on sequence, temperature, and molecular history. Each step defines a normalized distribution over structural tokens, giving explicit likelihoods for trajectories. It uses frame-isoentropic sampling to limit error accumulation during autoregressive generation.
AI.result: MD-LLM-2 reproduces median radius of gyration within 1 Angstrom in 10 of 12 unseen domains, predicts reduced Trp-cage compaction at higher temperature, and generates L99A T4 lysozyme trajectories reaching published transition-region structures. In alanine dipeptide, it predicts basin populations at unseen couplings with MAE 0.09 vs 0.35 (MBAR) and first-passage probabilities with error 0.08 vs 0.16 (Markov state model).
AI.conclusion: The framework extends MD-LLM from protein-specific generation to transferable, physically conditioned modelling with explicit path likelihoods, and can predict equilibrium populations for unseen force-field parameters, with initial evidence that first-passage kinetics can also be captured.

title: Toward Reliable Patient-Specific Aortic Strain Mapping from 4D CTA: Validation, Spectral Structure, and Clinical Potential
summary:
Objective: To develop and validate a framework for spatially resolved ascending aortic strain estimation from 4D computed tomography angiography (CTA) and characterize reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales.
  Methods: We constructed patient-specific aortic strain maps using nnU-Net segmentation, optimized surface remeshing, deformable registration, and mesh-based strain estimation. Finite element (FE)-derived synthetic 4D CT sequences provided controlled reference deformations for registration validation. Strain reliability was characterized across segmentation sources and Laplace-Beltrami (LB) spectral scales. Associations with diameter, aortic height index (AHI), and age were assessed.
  Results: Registration-derived median strain showed minimal bias relative to FE-reference strain for observer-derived (0.0013) and nnU-Net-derived meshes (0.0056). Median strain exhibited low bias and narrow 95% limits of agreement (LoA) across segmentation sources (interobserver: bias = -0.0045, LoA [-0.0490, 0.0399]; nnU-Net versus observer: bias = -0.0052, LoA [-0.0340, 0.0237]). Differences were greater for 95th-percentile strain, particularly in the interobserver comparison. LB spectral analysis showed preferential preservation of low-frequency strain organization, with k = 5 reconstructions reducing segmentation-related disagreement by 52-56%. The 95th-percentile areal strain was inversely associated with maximum ascending aortic diameter (r = -0.493, p = 0.005), AHI (r = -0.488, p = 0.005), and age (r = -0.479, p = 0.006). Three high-grade AR cases showed heterogeneous regional strain patterns.
  Conclusion: This framework reproducibly estimates ascending aortic strain from 4D CTA, characterizes its reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales, and demonstrates its potential for noninvasive assessment of patient-specific aortic mechanics.

AI.tldr: A framework for spatially resolved ascending aortic strain estimation from 4D CTA is developed and validated, showing high reproducibility, segmentation-source independence, and associations with aortic size and age.
AI.motivation: Noninvasive characterization of patient-specific ascending aortic mechanics is needed, yet reliable spatially resolved strain estimation from 4D CTA remains challenging across segmentation sources and spatial scales.
AI.method: Patient-specific aortic strain maps built via nnU-Net segmentation, optimized surface remeshing, deformable registration, and mesh-based strain estimation. FE-derived synthetic 4D CT sequences served as controlled references. Reliability assessed across segmentation sources and Laplace-Beltrami spectral scales; associations with diameter, AHI, and age examined.
AI.result: Registration-derived median strain showed minimal bias vs. FE reference (observer: 0.0013; nnU-Net: 0.0056) and low bias/narrow 95% LoA across segmentation sources. 95th-percentile strain differences were larger. LB spectral analysis preserved low-frequency organization, with k=5 reconstructions reducing segmentation-related disagreement by 52-56%. 95th-percentile areal strain inversely correlated with max diameter (r=-0.493), AHI (r=-0.488), and age (r=-0.479). Three high-grade AR cases showed heterogeneous regional patterns.
AI.conclusion: The framework reproducibly estimates ascending aortic strain from 4D CTA, characterizes reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales, and shows potential for noninvasive patient-specific aortic mechanics assessment.

title: Mean Field Theory Based on the Spike Time Response Curve for Synchronization Within and Between Two Alternating Populations of Neural Oscillators with Delays
summary: In order to study oscillators coupled by pulses emitted at discrete times, it is generally assumed that the effect of each pulse is an instantaneous phase shift, with a possible conduction delay between emission and receipt. However, we are interested in neural oscillators in which each pulse (action potential) activates a biexponential synapse, and at high frequencies, the duration of the synaptic conductance may be greater than the network period. Therefore, the effect of received pulses can summate over the course of several cycles. To overcome this limitation, we previously defined a mean field approach for a single synchronous population. Here, we extend it to two alternating synchronous populations by assuming a perturbation of a single oscillator from one of the synchronous populations which is represented by a single self-connected neural oscillator. The train of delayed biexponential synapses emitted by each oscillator is divided into a tonic and a phasic component. Because of the continuous rather than pulsatile nature of the input, we had to drop the concept of oscillator phase and derive self-consistent criteria for the existence and stability of an alternating firing pattern between two synchronous populations based solely on the perturbation of time intervals from their steady state values. Simulations showed that for high frequency oscillations as defined above, the mean field approach predicts the existence and stability of phase-locking between two synchronous populations better than the instantaneous phase shift approach. This approach may generalize to other forms of coupling amongst non-neural oscillators.

AI.tldr: A mean field approach is extended to two alternating synchronous neural populations, dropping the phase concept to derive self-consistent criteria for existence and stability of alternating firing patterns, outperforming the instantaneous phase shift approach at high frequencies.
AI.motivation: Standard pulse-coupled oscillator models assume each pulse causes an instantaneous phase shift, but in neural oscillators each action potential activates a biexponential synapse whose conductance may last longer than the network period at high frequencies. Effects of received pulses then summate across cycles, breaking the standard assumption.
AI.method: Extend a previously defined mean field approach from a single synchronous population to two alternating synchronous populations. A single oscillator from one population is modeled as a self-connected neural oscillator whose delayed biexponential synapse train is split into tonic and phasic components. Since input is continuous rather than pulsatile, the phase concept is dropped and self-consistent criteria for existence and stability of the alternating firing pattern are derived from perturbations of time intervals about steady state.
AI.result: Simulations showed that for high frequency oscillations, the mean field approach predicts the existence and stability of phase-locking between two synchronous populations better than the instantaneous phase shift approach.
AI.conclusion: The mean field method captures synaptic summation effects that the phase shift approach misses at high frequencies, and may generalize to other forms of coupling among non-neural oscillators.

title: If the brain were so simple: Information-based drivers of intelligence and their interaction through an n-body-inspired framework
summary: Theories of how the brain processes information and returns intelligent outputs are numerous and often difficult to conclusively test. Here, we consider an approach grounded in informatics and algorithmic thermodynamics for how neural systems respond to different patterns of information in different ways, with a focus on the relationship between the information entropy of a signal and a new proposed quantity we term information enthalpy, which represents the internal resource of structured information within a system available to be used for predictions and other forms of work. To evaluate the capacity of the external signals to increase information enthalpy in the system, we introduce the information enthalpy potential (IEP) as a defined metric. We propose and implement a method for quantifying the amount of potential information enthalpy - the IEP - in a given signal across a range of example signals. We offer a conjecture of how information enthalpy may be treated by neural systems within a biological framework before showing how it may integrate and offer falsifiability to existing approaches such as the Free Energy Principle. This framework is also positioned in light of the role of neural criticality. Finally, we postulate a testable and falsifiable framework where the distinct mechanisms within each driver interact through a described n-body-inspired model to govern the "motion" of a neural system through a high dimensional state-space. Through these processes, it is proposed that these features form the most fundamental basis of the neural drivers that give rise to the complexity of adaptive behaviors that are commonly called: intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes "information enthalpy" and an "information enthalpy potential" (IEP) metric, grounded in informatics and algorithmic thermodynamics, to quantify how neural systems extract structured information from signals. It connects this framework to the Free Energy Principle and neural criticality, and offers a falsifiable n-body-inspired model of neural dynamics in state-space as the basis of intelligence.
AI.motivation: Existing theories of how the brain processes information and produces intelligent outputs are numerous and often difficult to conclusively test, lacking a unified, falsifiable framework grounded in thermodynamic and informatic principles.
AI.method: The authors introduce information enthalpy (internal structured information usable for prediction/work) and define the information enthalpy potential (IEP). They develop and implement a method to quantify IEP across example signals, offer a biological conjecture, and propose an n-body-inspired model relating neural drivers.
AI.result: The method quantifies IEP in a range of example signals. The framework is shown to integrate with and offer falsifiability to existing approaches like the Free Energy Principle, and is positioned relative to neural criticality.
AI.conclusion: A testable, falsifiable framework is proposed in which distinct neural drivers interact via an n-body-inspired model to govern neural motion through a high-dimensional state-space, argued to form the fundamental basis of adaptive behavior and intelligence.

title: Cross-species representation learning aligns mouse and human neural dynamics and tracks clinical drug efficacy
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included (2 supplementary figures, 3 supplementary tables)
summary: Preclinical models poorly predict human drug efficacy, particularly in neurological disorders. Neural activity offers a uniquely rich source of translational information because it captures high-dimensional variation in nervous-system function that can be measured in both animals and humans. However, its high dimensionality makes it difficult to distinguish conserved disease-related features from variation arising from species, recording modality and experimental context. Here, we test whether shared neural dynamics can be identified directly from electrophysiology data by learning representations organized by biological state rather than species. We develop a dual-rule contrastive learning framework that aligns corresponding mouse and human states while preserving separation between distinct phenotypes. This framework recovered conserved sensory-response structure across species and, in epilepsy, resolved distinct relationships between three mouse models and heterogeneous human patient populations. When treated animals were projected into a frozen cross-species representation, drug-induced movement towards the human-aligned healthy state retrospectively tracked known clinical efficacy across ten model-drug combinations including a disease-specific detrimental effect. The framework also identified shared disease-associated neural dynamics between Fmr1-knockout mice and human 16p11.2 copy-number variant carriers despite differences in genetic aetiology and recording modality. Together, these findings show the potential of cross-species neural representation learning to map heterogeneous human disease onto experimentally tractable preclinical states and assess whether interventions restore human-relevant circuit function.

AI.tldr: A dual-rule contrastive learning framework learns cross-species neural representations organized by biological state (not species), aligning mouse and human electrophysiology to recover conserved disease-related dynamics and predict drug efficacy.
AI.motivation: Preclinical models poorly predict human drug efficacy, especially in neurological disorders. Neural activity is a rich translational signal but its high dimensionality makes it hard to separate conserved disease features from species, modality, and context confounds.
AI.method: The authors developed a dual-rule contrastive learning framework that aligns corresponding mouse and human biological states while preserving separation between distinct phenotypes, learning representations organized by state rather than species.
AI.result: The framework recovered conserved sensory-response structure across species, resolved relationships between three mouse epilepsy models and heterogeneous human patients, tracked known clinical efficacy across ten model-drug combinations (including a detrimental effect), and identified shared disease dynamics between Fmr1-knockout mice and human 16p11.2 CNV carriers.
AI.conclusion: Cross-species neural representation learning can map heterogeneous human disease onto tractable preclinical states and assess whether interventions restore human-relevant circuit function.

title: Elucidating the Space of Enzymatic Reaction: A Unified Benchmark and Pretrained Model
summary: Existing reaction models primarily learn molecular transformations, whereas enzy- matic reactions depend jointly on molecular structure and catalytic function. We formulate this problem as learning an enzymatic reaction space linking reactants, products, and Enzyme Commission (EC) annotations. To characterize this space, we introduce VenusRX-Bench, a unified benchmark for forward reaction prediction, single-step retrosynthesis, and EC-number prediction. VenusRX-Bench integrates reactions from multiple biochemical databases with standardized curation, leakage- controlled splits, and consistent evaluation. Benchmarking representative chemical and enzymatic models reveals a clear chemical-to-enzymatic domain gap, driven by limited domain data, catalytic-context dependency, and the difficulty of modeling large biomolecular structures. To bridge this gap, we develop VenusRX, a unified T5-style sequence-to-sequence model for enzymatic reactions. VenusRX jointly learns forward prediction, ret- rosynthesis, and reaction reconstruction, with two-stage training on millions of template-expanded reactions followed by real biochemical reactions. In addition, optional EC conditioning incorporates catalytic context, while Molecule Library- Constrained Decoding improves the generation of complex biomolecules. Across benchmark tasks and challenging generalization splits, VenusRX achieves the best or competitive performance on most evaluated settings over representative chem- ical and enzymatic baselines. Moreover, EC information consistently improves reaction prediction, while learned reaction representations support accurate EC prediction, revealing a bidirectional relationship between reaction structure and catalytic function. Together, VenusRX-Bench and VenusRX provide a unified framework for elucidating and modeling enzymatic reaction space

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VenusRX-Bench, a unified benchmark for enzymatic reactions (forward prediction, retrosynthesis, EC prediction), and VenusRX, a T5-based seq2seq model that bridges the chemical-to-enzymatic domain gap.
AI.motivation: Existing reaction models learn molecular transformations but ignore that enzymatic reactions depend jointly on molecular structure and catalytic function. There lacks a unified benchmark to characterize enzymatic reaction space and to reveal the chemical-to-enzymatic domain gap.
AI.method: VenusRX-Bench integrates multiple biochemical databases with standardized curation, leakage-controlled splits, and consistent evaluation. VenusRX is a unified T5-style seq2seq model jointly learning forward prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction reconstruction, with two-stage training (millions of template-expanded then real reactions), optional EC conditioning, and Molecule Library-Constrained Decoding.
AI.result: VenusRX achieves best or competitive performance on most evaluated settings over representative chemical and enzymatic baselines, including challenging generalization splits. EC information consistently improves reaction prediction, and learned representations support accurate EC prediction.
AI.conclusion: EC information and reaction structure exhibit a bidirectional relationship. VenusRX-Bench and VenusRX together provide a unified framework for elucidating and modeling enzymatic reaction space.

title: Neural Decoding as Cognitive Inference
summary: The brain maintains stable cognition despite continuously changing neural activity. How to extract stable cognitive states from variable neural observations remains a central problem in neural decoding. Existing neural decoding methods map neural observations to predefined external labels based on the stimulus-response principle, often capturing recording-specific spurious correlations. Inspired by how the brain infers the world, and specifically by Bayesian brain theory, we recast neural decoding as cognitive inference constrained by brain-intrinsic priors, yielding high-level meta-neural semantic representations. In decoding experiments spanning five neural recording modalities and three cognitive domains (motor, perception and internal mentation), our cognitive inference method reorganized the geometry of neural observation representations, yielding meta-neural semantic representations that exhibited consistent geometric relationships across cognitive tasks and enabled the recovery of stable cognitive states from variable neural observations. Our work provides an account of how the brain maintains relatively stable cognition despite continual changes in the external environment. Cognitive stability is sustained through cognitive inference from changing neural activity, without requiring fixed neural activity patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes neural decoding as Bayesian cognitive inference constrained by brain-intrinsic priors, producing stable meta-neural semantic representations that recover consistent cognitive states across five neural recording modalities and three cognitive domains.
AI.motivation: The brain maintains stable cognition despite continuously changing neural activity, but existing neural decoding methods map observations to predefined external labels via the stimulus-response principle, capturing recording-specific spurious correlations and failing to yield stable cognitive states from variable neural observations.
AI.method: Inspired by Bayesian brain theory, neural decoding is recast as cognitive inference constrained by brain-intrinsic priors, yielding high-level meta-neural semantic representations rather than direct observation-to-label mappings.
AI.result: Across five neural recording modalities and three cognitive domains (motor, perception, internal mentation), the method reorganized the geometry of neural observation representations, producing meta-neural semantic representations with consistent geometric relationships across tasks and enabling recovery of stable cognitive states from variable observations.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive stability is sustained through cognitive inference from changing neural activity without requiring fixed neural activity patterns, offering an account of how the brain maintains relatively stable cognition despite a continually changing external environment.

title: La-Ribo: RNA Co-Design via Geometry-Latent Flow Matching
summary: RNA function arises from the coupling of nucleotide sequence and three-dimensional structure, motivating their joint design. Coordinating global folding with nucleotide-level detail remains challenging under limited structural supervision. We introduce La-Ribo, a generative framework for RNA sequence-structure co-design via geometry-latent flow matching. La-Ribo retains a sparse phosphate-sugar--base scaffold and encodes nucleotide identity and local conformation in residue-wise latents. A shared flow network generates both jointly, and an RNA-specific decoder then reconstructs all heavy atoms. To expand supervision, we construct a quality-controlled corpus of 168,561 RNA structures, integrating experimental data with predictions from three folding models, including 10,631 MSA-supported structures generated in this work. La-Ribo improves designability and codesignability over the evaluated baselines across sampling budgets and two refolding models, and the same prior supports scaffold-conditioned inverse folding without additional training.

AI.tldr: La-Ribo is a generative framework for joint RNA sequence-structure co-design using geometry-latent flow matching, supported by a large quality-controlled structural corpus.
AI.motivation: RNA function depends on the coupling of nucleotide sequence and 3D structure, so designing them jointly is desirable. However, coordinating global folding with nucleotide-level detail is hard given limited structural supervision.
AI.method: La-Ribo uses geometry-latent flow matching: it keeps a sparse phosphate-sugar-base scaffold, encodes nucleotide identity and local conformation in residue-wise latents, and a shared flow network generates both jointly. An RNA-specific decoder reconstructs all heavy atoms. A corpus of 168,561 RNA structures was built, combining experimental data with predictions from three folding models, including 10,631 MSA-supported structures.
AI.result: La-Ribo improves designability and co-designability over evaluated baselines across sampling budgets and two refolding models. The same prior also supports scaffold-conditioned inverse folding without additional training.
AI.conclusion: La-Ribo enables effective joint RNA sequence-structure co-design with limited structural supervision, extending to inverse folding tasks.

title: Unlocking the Regulatory Genome by ARGUS: An Evidence-Constrained Agentic Framework for Interpreting Single Nucleotide Variants
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic AI for Biological Discovery (AgenticLS). Code: https://github.com/duttaprat/ARGUS
summary: Over 90% of disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies fall in noncoding regulatory regions, yet their functional interpretation remains a central open problem in genomic medicine. Large language models prompted to interpret such variants routinely hallucinate transcription factor (TF) binding changes, fabricate experimental support, and assign biological significance to statistically negligible signals. We present ARGUS (Agentic Regulatory Genomics for an Uncertainty-aware Scientist), which strictly separates deterministic biological computation from LLM-mediated reasoning. ARGUS wraps 458 DNABERT-based TF binding models in a hypothesis-directed investigation loop where a planner selects evidence sources based on current uncertainty, a verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and intermediate results change the investigation path. On variant rs6983267 at the 8q24 cancer risk locus, the same planner produces four divergent trajectories for four TFs. FOXA1 is rescued in 3 steps when real ADASTRA allele-specific binding data (15 experiments, FDR = 0.030) reveals a model false negative masked by saturation. KLF6 traverses 8 steps across ADASTRA, JASPAR motif analysis, and ENCODE cCRE regulatory annotation before abstaining due to mixed indirect evidence. RAD21 abstains in 8 steps after ADASTRA returns a coverage-qualified but nonsignificant allelic test (5 experiments, FDR = 0.65), and SP1, which shares FOXA1's saturated retained prediction, abstains because no direct experimental evidence exists at this locus. All observations come from real ADASTRA, JASPAR, and ENCODE cCRE queries; none are simulated. A comparison of fixed-priority and LLM-mediated planning shows that the LLM planner reaches identical verdicts with fewer tool calls by declining evidence that cannot resolve the claim under test.

AI.tldr: ARGUS is an agentic framework that separates deterministic TF binding computation from LLM reasoning, using uncertainty-directed investigation to interpret noncoding variants without hallucination.
AI.motivation: Over 90% of GWAS disease-associated variants lie in noncoding regulatory regions, and LLMs prompted to interpret them routinely hallucinate TF binding changes, fabricate experimental support, and overstate negligible signals.
AI.method: ARGUS wraps 458 DNABERT-based TF binding models in a hypothesis-directed loop: a planner picks evidence sources by current uncertainty, a verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and results redirect the investigation. It uses real ADASTRA, JASPAR, and ENCODE cCRE queries.
AI.result: On rs6983267 (8q24), four TFs yield four distinct trajectories: FOXA1 rescued in 3 steps via ADASTRA allele-specific binding (15 experiments, FDR=0.030); KLF6 abstains after 8 steps of mixed indirect evidence; RAD21 abstains after nonsignificant ADASTRA test (5 experiments, FDR=0.65); SP1 abstains due to no direct evidence. LLM planning matches fixed-priority verdicts with fewer tool calls.
AI.conclusion: Strictly separating deterministic computation from LLM reasoning enables uncertainty-aware, evidence-grounded regulatory variant interpretation, with LLM planning improving efficiency by declining uninformative evidence.

title: A minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction
summary: Rate-induced tipping ("R-tipping") in ecological modelling is characterised by too-rapid change of an environmental parameter causing collapse of a population without any bifurcation being crossed ("B-tipping"). A well-known example of a slow-fast predator-prey model in which R-tipping is observed [Vanselow, Wieczorek, Feudel, Journal of Theoretical Biology, 479, 64-72 (2019)] suffers from unecological "resurgence", whereby populations driven to functional extinction recover towards stable coexistence. We propose an analytically tractable model, incorporating a strong Allee effect into the prey dynamics in a slow-fast Lotka-Volterra-type predator-prey system, which induces bistability and thus renders the extinction state a genuine attractor. Applying geometric singular perturbation theory (GSPT), we describe the dynamics of the extended model that is obtained by "ramping" of the inverse prey carrying capacity. We show the presence of a parabolic-shaped, folded critical manifold which admits a folded saddle singularity, the strong canard of which separates solutions that track the moving coexistence state from those that tip to extinction. The analytical simplicity of our model allows us to derive explicit expressions for the critical rate that separates "tracking" from "tipping" dynamics. Finally, we argue that our system represents a minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction, in that it incorporates three essential ingredients: bistability, a folded critical manifold, and a folded-saddle-type canard.

AI.tldr: A minimal slow-fast predator-prey model with a strong Allee effect in the prey yields a genuine extinction attractor and shows rate-induced tipping (R-tipping) driven by a folded-saddle canard on a folded critical manifold.
AI.motivation: Existing slow-fast predator-prey models exhibiting R-tipping (e.g., Vanselow et al. 2019) suffer from unecological "resurgence," where functionally extinct populations recover to coexistence. The authors seek a more ecologically realistic model where extinction is a true attractor and tipping to extinction is genuine.
AI.method: They incorporate a strong Allee effect into prey dynamics within a slow-fast Lotka-Volterra-type predator-prey system, inducing bistability and making the extinction state a genuine attractor. They ramp the inverse prey carrying capacity and apply geometric singular perturbation theory (GSPT), analyzing the folded critical manifold, folded saddle singularity, and its strong canard.
AI.result: The model features a parabolic folded critical manifold admitting a folded saddle whose strong canard separates tracking solutions from tipping-to-extinction solutions. Analytically tractable, it yields explicit expressions for the critical rate separating "tracking" from "tipping" dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The system is argued to be a minimal model for rate-induced tipping to extinction, requiring three essential ingredients: bistability, a folded critical manifold, and a folded-saddle-type canard.

title: Learning infinite context windows in recurrent architectures via spatial neural computing
summary: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) offer linear-time scaling with sequence length while requiring only constant memory, yet they struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to vanishing gradients and limited receptive fields. To address these limitations, we introduce a second-order recurrent model in which the standard neuron-to-neuron communication is replaced by a spatially evolving field governed by (discretized) partial differential equations. Drawing inspiration from the role of cortical waves in brain computation, this mechanism allows structured spatiotemporal patterns to serve as an implicit, high-capacity memory. We show that the resulting model is equivalent to a structured infinite-order RNN in which the current state depends explicitly on its entire history of past states, yielding an effectively unbounded receptive field with a fixed number of parameters. We further derive constructive conditions to ensure marginal stability, constraining the gradient spectrum on the unit circle and thereby eliminating vanishing and exploding gradients. Empirically, the proposed architecture outperforms other recurrent models on long-horizon benchmarks while using substantially fewer parameters, demonstrating that spatial dynamics can effectively bridge the gap between efficient inference and long-term memory.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a second-order recurrent model that replaces neuron-to-neuron communication with a spatially evolving field governed by discretized PDEs, inspired by cortical waves, achieving infinite-order recurrence with unbounded receptive field under fixed parameters.
AI.motivation: RNNs scale linearly with sequence length and use constant memory, but suffer from vanishing gradients and limited receptive fields, making it hard to capture long-range dependencies. The authors aim to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: Replace standard neuron-to-neuron communication with a spatially evolving field governed by discretized PDEs, inspired by cortical waves in brain computation. This yields structured spatiotemporal patterns as implicit high-capacity memory. They show equivalence to a structured infinite-order RNN where current state depends on its entire past-state history, and derive constructive conditions for marginal stability by constraining the gradient spectrum on the unit circle.
AI.result: The model achieves an effectively unbounded receptive field with a fixed number of parameters, eliminating vanishing and exploding gradients. Empirically, it outperforms other recurrent models on long-horizon benchmarks while using substantially fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Spatial dynamics can effectively bridge the gap between efficient inference and long-term memory.

title: Similar Predictive Fit but Different Latent Dynamics: Characterizing Learned Dynamical Structure in Personalized Models of Brain Disorders
comment: Accepted at the World Models for High-Stakes Health (WMHS) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: As AI models move toward clinical decision-making and personalized treatment, understanding \emph{what} a model learns is important beyond predictive accuracy alone. We investigate whether personalized latent dynamics reveal clinically associated differences even when predictive fit is similar. A lightweight CNN--Transformer EEG foundation model pretrained on the Temple University EEG Corpus (TUEG) extracts segment-level representations. Using the Temple University Epilepsy Corpus (TUEP), representations are mapped to a shared latent-state space, and sparse multinomial logistic transition distributions (mLTD) are fit independently to each subject to obtain personalized transition-dependency graphs $W_n$. Analyses include $n{=}198$ subjects (99 epilepsy / 99 non-epilepsy). At $k{=}4$, epilepsy subjects exhibit substantially denser learned dependency structure ($p{=}1.1\times10^{-7}$), with the same pattern at $k{=}6$ (19.90 vs. 13.46; $p{=}5.2\times10^{-5}$). Graph-derived features provide moderate group discrimination under 5-fold subject-wise cross-validation (AUROC 0.68 at $k{=}4$; 0.65 at $k{=}6$). In contrast, held-out log-likelihood is nearly identical between groups at $k{=}4$ ($-0.992$ vs. $-0.991$; $p{=}0.95$), with similarly matched next-state prediction (AUROC 0.855 vs. 0.861; $p{=}0.54$). Thus, similar predictive fit does not imply similar learned dynamics: groups can be comparably predictable while differing substantially in the internal dynamical structure learned by personalized models. This distinction motivates evaluating learned structure alongside predictive performance in personalized clinical models.

AI.tldr: Personalized latent dynamics from an EEG foundation model reveal clear clinical group differences in learned structure even when predictive fit is nearly identical.
AI.motivation: As AI moves toward clinical decision-making, accuracy alone is insufficient; we need to understand what a model learns. The paper asks whether personalized latent dynamics expose clinically associated differences even when predictive fit is similar.
AI.method: A lightweight CNN–Transformer EEG foundation model pretrained on TUEG extracts segment-level representations. Using TUEP, representations are mapped to a shared latent-state space, and sparse multinomial logistic transition distributions (mLTD) are fit per subject to obtain personalized transition-dependency graphs W_n. 198 subjects (99 epilepsy / 99 non-epilepsy) analyzed at k=4 and k=6.
AI.result: Epilepsy subjects show substantially denser dependency structure at k=4 (p=1.1e-7) and k=6 (19.90 vs 13.46; p=5.2e-5). Graph features give moderate discrimination (AUROC 0.68 at k=4, 0.65 at k=6). Yet held-out log-likelihood is nearly identical (k=4: -0.992 vs -0.991; p=0.95), and next-state prediction is matched (AUROC 0.855 vs 0.861; p=0.54).
AI.conclusion: Similar predictive fit does not imply similar learned dynamics: groups can be comparably predictable while differing in internal dynamical structure. Learned structure should be evaluated alongside predictive performance in personalized clinical models.

title: Predictive Multiplicity in Cell-Fate Assignment: Label-Free Rashomon Sets and the Limits of Per-Cell Certification
summary: Single-cell trajectory inference maps transcriptomic measurements onto developmental continua, yet configurations that fit the data equally well can assign conflicting cell fates. FateMultiplicity is a label-free framework that constructs a statistically admissible model set, or Rashomon set, without lineage labels, by evaluating model discrepancy on cross-fitted held-out genes under non-inferiority testing calibrated against random-seed variation. Multiplicity is large and depends more on the diversity of the model space than its size: twelve configurations of a second algorithm expose 20.0% of cells where twenty-four of the first expose 3.8%. Whether the per-cell certified fate margin FM yields more reliable assignments than the fitted model already provides is then tested, and it does not. On simulation ground truth, on the same cells, FM discriminates misassignment at AUC 0.682, against 0.965 for the baseline configuration's own decision margin (p = 0.003) and 0.854 for a seed-dispersion baseline. Informativeness is governed by the breadth of the admitted set, not its cardinality: at cardinality four, seed refits give 0.933 and hyperparameter-perturbed sets 0.701. Relaxing the infimum to a q-quantile recovers discrimination but converges toward the single model's own confidence; the supremum reaches 0.973 because theta*'s membership bounds it from below, while the infimum is unanchored. Multiplicity in trajectory inference is worth measuring and reporting, but per-cell certification over a label-free Rashomon set is not a route to more reliable fate calls. Two constructions survive: a margin-erosion ratio separates real from spurious branch points in simulation (AUC 0.890, untested on real data), and against clonally observed fate, uncertified cells disagree with their clone's outcome 16.4 percentage points more often than certified cells (p < 0.001).

AI.tldr: FateMultiplicity builds a label-free Rashomon set to measure model multiplicity in single-cell trajectory inference; multiplicity is large and diversity-driven, but per-cell certification does not yield more reliable fate calls.
AI.motivation: Trajectory inference can map cells onto developmental continua, but equally well-fitting configurations can assign conflicting cell fates. There is a need to quantify this multiplicity and test whether certification from a label-free model set improves fate assignment reliability.
AI.method: A label-free framework constructing a statistically admissible Rashomon set without lineage labels, using model discrepancy on cross-fitted held-out genes under non-inferiority testing calibrated against random-seed variation. It compares a per-cell certified fate margin (FM) against baselines including the fitted model's decision margin and seed dispersion, and examines margin-erosion ratio and clonal disagreement.
AI.result: Multiplicity depends more on model-space diversity than size: 12 configurations of one algorithm expose 20.0% of cells where 24 of another expose 3.8%. FM underperforms: AUC 0.682 vs 0.965 for the baseline decision margin (p=0.003) and 0.854 for seed dispersion. Informativeness tracks set breadth, not cardinality (0.933 seed refits vs 0.701 hyperparameter-perturbed at cardinality four). Margin-erosion ratio separates real from spurious branch points (AUC 0.890), and uncertified cells disagree with clonal fate 16.4 pp more often (p<0.001).
AI.conclusion: Multiplicity in trajectory inference is worth measuring and reporting, but per-cell certification over a label-free Rashomon set is not a route to more reliable fate calls. Two constructions survive: margin-erosion ratio for branch-point separation and clonal disagreement for uncertified cells.

title: Beyond Action Entropy: Quotient-Space Exploration for Genome-Scale Metabolic Model Repair
summary: Repairing scientific models from functional observations differs fundamentally from supervised prediction: feedback may certify a solution without revealing which structural correction is responsible. We study this setting for genome-scale metabolic model (GEM) repair, where multiple reaction edits can explain the same phenotypes and many apparently distinct edits correspond to the same biological mechanism. This many-to-one structure creates a hidden failure mode for conventional exploration: diversity in the output space need not translate into diversity of scientific hypotheses. We introduce QuotientPO, which collapses equivalent repairs into canonical mechanisms and optimizes exploration directly over the resulting quotient space. To make quotient exploration informative under finite rollouts, we derive a kernelized Rényi estimator that resolves graded crowding among distinct repair cores beyond coarse exact-match counts. On 2,212 held-out GEMs, QuotientPO improves Success@32 from 17.93% to 20.10% (+12.1% relative) while consistently increasing distinct successful-core discovery under the same sampling budget. These results establish quotient-space exploration as a principled approach to mechanism-level discovery under verifier-induced equivalence.

AI.tldr: QuotientPO repairs genome-scale metabolic models by collapsing equivalent reaction edits into canonical mechanisms and exploring directly over this quotient space, using a kernelized Rényi estimator for graded diversity. It improves Success@32 from 17.93% to 20.10%.
AI.motivation: Repairing scientific models from functional observations is not supervised prediction: feedback certifies a solution without revealing the responsible correction. In GEM repair, many distinct edits map to the same mechanism, so output-space diversity need not reflect hypothesis diversity—a hidden failure mode for conventional exploration.
AI.method: QuotientPO collapses equivalent repairs into canonical mechanisms and optimizes exploration over the resulting quotient space. A kernelized Rényi estimator is derived to resolve graded crowding among distinct repair cores under finite rollouts.
AI.result: On 2,212 held-out GEMs, QuotientPO raises Success@32 from 17.93% to 20.10% (+12.1% relative) and consistently increases distinct successful-core discovery at the same sampling budget.
AI.conclusion: Quotient-space exploration is a principled approach to mechanism-level discovery under verifier-induced equivalence.

title: Certified Scalable Enclosures for Uncertain Underdetermined Systems
summary: The central challenge in underdetermined models with bounded uncertainty, such as in nonlinear design and estimation, is certifying the solution sets. Conventional solution methodologies, such as those based on Newton's method or on sampling-based uncertainty quantification, are either not applicable due to the underdetermined nature or do not give guarantees that all solutions have been found, assuming they converge. We addressed this issue for a problem that arises in nonlinear design, where a target steady-state box is prescribed and the parameters have to be found. We developed a trapezoidal linearisation method that rigorously encloses all solutions and combined it with a tractable linear programming method to compute the component-wise bounds. We showed that the resulting families of linear programs can iteratively contract an initial parameter region. A subdivision of the target state and the initial parameter region can improve the contraction and provide tighter enclosures. The trapezoidal relaxation gives a family of linear programs that can also be used for finding solutions for interval linear systems via the Oettli-Prager characterisation. We demonstrate the generality of the method through different applications, including nonlinear design in biomolecular circuits, a sensitivity analysis method, and in a compressed sensing context, and discuss the trade-off between enclosure tightness and computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a trapezoidal linearisation method combined with linear programming to rigorously enclose all solutions of underdetermined models with bounded uncertainty, particularly for nonlinear design problems with a prescribed steady-state box.
AI.motivation: Conventional solution methods (Newton's method, sampling-based uncertainty quantification) fail for underdetermined models with bounded uncertainty: they are either inapplicable or cannot guarantee that all solutions are found. This leaves solution set certification in nonlinear design and estimation unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors develop a trapezoidal linearisation method that rigorously encloses all solutions of the parameter-finding problem. This is combined with a tractable linear programming method to compute component-wise bounds. The resulting families of linear programs iteratively contract an initial parameter region, with subdivision of the target state and initial parameter region improving contraction and tightening enclosures.
AI.result: The trapezoidal relaxation yields linear programs that can also find solutions for interval linear systems via the Oettli-Prager characterisation. The method is demonstrated on nonlinear design in biomolecular circuits, a sensitivity analysis method, and a compressed sensing context, with a discussion of the trade-off between enclosure tightness and computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides rigorous enclosure of all solutions for underdetermined models with bounded uncertainty and is general enough to apply across diverse domains, offering controllable trade-offs between solution tightness and computational effort.

title: Persistence of bounded trajectories in positively transverse reaction networks
summary: We introduce positively transverse reaction networks and show that, with mass-action kinetics, no bounded trajectory with positive initial condition has a boundary omega-limit point. These networks are characterized by a geometric property of a collection of polytopes defined by a subset of complexes of the network.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces positively transverse reaction networks and proves that under mass-action kinetics, bounded trajectories with positive initial conditions cannot have boundary omega-limit points.
AI.motivation: Earlier work on autonomous oscillator networks and toric dynamical systems suggested the need to distinguish oscillator-like behavior in various classes. Here the authors investigate conditions under which the boundary of the phase space (where some species are exhausted) cannot attract bounded trajectories.
AI.method: The authors define a class of reaction networks via a geometric condition on a collection of polytopes built from subsets of the network complexes. For mass-action kinetics, they use this geometric property to rule out boundary accumulation points of bounded positive trajectories.
AI.result: It is shown that for positively transverse reaction networks with mass-action kinetics, a bounded trajectory with a positive initial condition has no boundary point as an omega-limit point.
AI.conclusion: Positive transversality provides a geometric criterion guaranteeing that persistent, bounded mass-action trajectories remain away from the boundary.

title: Three-dimensional imaging of isolated membrane-protein complexes in vacuo with an X-ray laser
summary: The prospect of imaging single biomolecules, viruses and cells with intense, ultrashort X-ray pulses has driven the development of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs). However, the weak scattering from small particles is easily swamped by background from residual gas, which has so far limited applications to strongly scattering targets such as viruses, cell organelles and cells. Here we report a three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of an isolated 1-MDa membrane-protein complex, photosystem I (PS I), from single-particle diffraction data. PS I trimers were aerosolised by charge-reduction electrospray ionisation and injected into the European XFEL beam, with partial helium gas exchange reducing background scattering by 80%. From 32 788 diffraction patterns of single trimers in random orientations, we reconstructed the 3D electron density to a resolution of 3.8 nm, limited by the detector geometry. The disc-shaped density, about 22 nm across and 10 nm thick, matches the size of a PS I trimer in a detergent micelle and is consistent with the compaction predicted by molecular dynamics simulations of the complex in vacuo and observed in native mass spectrometry. These results show that membrane-protein complexes can be imaged in vacuo with X-ray lasers, an important step towards ultrafast diffractive imaging of single macromolecules.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a 3D reconstruction of an isolated 1-MDa membrane-protein complex (photosystem I) using single-particle X-ray diffraction at the European XFEL, achieving 3.8 nm resolution with reduced background scattering.
AI.motivation: XFELs enable imaging of single biomolecules, but weak scattering from small particles is overwhelmed by background from residual gas, limiting applications to strongly scattering targets like viruses and cells.
AI.method: PS I trimers were aerosolised by charge-reduction electrospray ionisation and injected into the European XFEL beam, with partial helium gas exchange reducing background scattering by 80%. 3D electron density was reconstructed from 32,788 diffraction patterns of single trimers in random orientations.
AI.result: A 3D reconstruction was achieved at 3.8 nm resolution, limited by detector geometry. The disc-shaped density (~22 nm across, ~10 nm thick) matches the size of a PS I trimer in a detergent micelle and is consistent with in vacuo compacting predicted by molecular dynamics and observed in native mass spectrometry.
AI.conclusion: Membrane-protein complexes can be imaged in vacuo with X-ray lasers, an important step towards ultrafast diffractive imaging of single macromolecules.

title: Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks
summary: The Lyapunov spectrum of a nonlinear recurrent neural network with random asymmetric couplings is calculated in the limit $N\to\infty$. The calculation is based on a finite-$N$ identity that expresses the cumulative distribution of Lyapunov exponents as a response function of the tangent-space dynamics, with the tangent trajectory selected by a minimum-norm condition rather than by an initial condition. A cavity method then determines this response function at large $N$ through a self-consistent single-site problem. This result establishes that the chaos in this network is extensive and gives access to diffeomorphism-invariant properties of the dynamics. This work was done in collaboration with the AI models GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5.

AI.tldr: The paper computes the full Lyapunov spectrum of a nonlinear recurrent neural network with random asymmetric couplings in the N→∞ limit using a cavity method built on a finite-N identity, establishing extensive chaos.
AI.motivation: Understanding chaos in random recurrent neural networks is central to neuroscience and statistical physics, but prior work largely characterized only the largest Lyapunov exponent. A full Lyapunov spectrum was lacking, limiting access to invariant properties of the dynamics.
AI.method: A finite-N identity expresses the cumulative distribution of Lyapunov exponents as a response function of the tangent-space dynamics, with the tangent trajectory chosen via a minimum-norm condition instead of an initial condition. A cavity method then determines this response function at large N through a self-consistent single-site problem.
AI.result: The complete Lyapunov spectrum is obtained in the N→∞ limit, showing that chaos in this network is extensive. The approach also provides access to diffeomorphism-invariant properties of the dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The cavity-based framework yields the full Lyapunov spectrum for random asymmetric recurrent networks, confirms extensive chaos, and offers a route to invariant dynamical properties. The work was done in collaboration with the AI models GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5.
